slides.title: Musamir is too slow at the evening peak and too costly
slides.text: The case study Musamir is too slow at the evening peak and too costly Liwan National Events Authority (fictional) runs Musamir, a bilingual visitor assistant. Three tenants share it: Qamra Festival, Sawt Concerts, Athar Heritage Week. One leased L4 accelerator serves Qwen3-8B in 16 bits. 40,000 synthetic requests a day; 7,656 in the busiest hour; 55% Arabic; 18% ask about long event terms. The complaint Visitors wait, answers crawl, and the lease is the largest line of the digital services budget. Dr. Hanadi Al-Kathiri wants the objective met at a cost she can defend.

slides.title: The prompt is read in one pass; the answer is written one token at a time
slides.text: One request, two phases The prompt is read in one pass; the answer is written one token at a time 1 · Prompt 2,000 tokens arrive → 2 · Prefill all 2,000 in one pass → 3 · First token the visitor sees a reply start → 4 · Decode one pass per token Two phases, two bottlenecks. Prefill does a lot of work per byte read; decode does almost none.

slides.title: A token costs about two operations per weight, and a read of every weight
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · task 2 A token costs about two operations per weight, and a read of every weight Model Operations per token Bytes read per step (16-bit) Operations per byte Qwen3-8B (base) 15.14 G 16.40 GB 0.92 Musamir-mini (1.7B student) 3.42 G 3.40 GB 1.01 Operations: 2 × (non-embedding parameters + the output head, hidden size × vocabulary). Bytes: every parameter, 2 bytes each.

slides.title: Below the ridge a step waits on memory; above it, on arithmetic
slides.text: The roofline Below the ridge a step waits on memory; above it, on arithmetic Intensity = operations ÷ bytes moved. Ridge point = reachable operations per second ÷ reachable bytes per second. On the L4: 121 dense BF16 TFLOPS at 45%, 300 GB/s at 80%: 227 operations per byte. The sheet prints 242 TFLOPS with sparsity; dense is half. Recap from AE-206 The roofline of a layer and the efficiencies of an accelerator are in AE-206, Day 1. Here we apply it to the two phases of a language model.

slides.title: Every token leaves a key and a value in every layer
slides.text: The cache Every token leaves a key and a value in every layer kv_per_token = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes # = 2 * 36 * 8 * 128 * 2 # = 147,456 bytes = 144 KiB per token A 2,000-token conversation holds 0.29 GB of cache while it is served.

slides.title: Grouped-query attention cut the cache by four
slides.text: Read the model card Grouped-query attention cut the cache by four 32 query heads Used during the step, never stored. 8 key-value heads Stored for every token: the cache is a quarter of what 32 heads would need. What goes wrong. Sizing with num_attention_heads overestimates the cache four times and underestimates concurrency four times.

slides.title: The engine hands out the cache in blocks of 16 tokens
slides.text: Paged cache The engine hands out the cache in blocks of 16 tokens A conversation takes blocks as it grows, not a slab sized for the longest possible answer. Musamir's engine reports 1,525 blocks = 24,400 tokens at start. Blocks can be shared between requests with the same beginning: Day 2's prefix cache. When no block is free, a running sequence is preempted and recomputed later.

slides.title: A full cache preempts during decoding, not only at admission
slides.text: Preemption A full cache preempts during decoding, not only at admission Every answer token needs room; at 16 tokens a block, a sequence asks for a new block every 16 tokens. No free block: the engine frees the newest sequence and recomputes it later. The visitor sees it as a sudden stall, and the work is done twice. Seeded fault 2 Tomorrow you meet a deployment that preempts all evening. This slide is how you will recognise it.

slides.title: Four clocks per request, and the objective uses three of them
slides.text: What a visitor feels Four clocks per request, and the objective uses three of them TTFT From sending to the first token: any upload, then queue plus prefill. TPOT Per token after the first: the reading pace. Longest stall The largest gap between two tokens: the freeze. End to end The whole answer; not in the objective.

slides.title: Goodput counts only the requests that met the whole objective
slides.text: The measure of this course Goodput counts only the requests that met the whole objective met = (df.ttft_s <= 2.0) & (df.tpot_s <= 0.150) & (df.stall_s <= 1.0) goodput = met.sum() / (df.end.max() - df.start.min()) attainment = met.mean() Throughput counts every finished request. Goodput counts the visitors who were served well.

slides.title: Concurrency is the number of visitors waiting for an answer at once
slides.text: Load Concurrency is the number of visitors waiting for an answer at once Closed loop : each user sends the next request when the last answer ends, so the load is a number of users, not a rate. Easy to control and repeat, which is why curves are drawn over it. Kinder than reality: when the engine slows, the users slow too.

slides.title: Seven points, three runs each, raw rows kept
A curve is evidence only if someone else can rerun it
slides.text: Benchmark validity A curve is evidence only if someone else can rerun it The same trace, or a named sample of it, with its seed. Warm-up dropped: the first 10% of each run here. Enough requests per point to fill the engine many times. Three or more repeats, and the spread reported. The raw per-request rows kept beside the plot. The configuration and the engine version recorded. The objectives written on the plot. Closed or open loop stated.

A closed-loop test at "high concurrency" can look survivable while real arrivals would grow the queue without bound.

slides.title: The engine rebuilds the batch at every step, not every request
slides.text: Continuous batching The engine rebuilds the batch at every step, not every request Step one forward pass Finished? leave the batch at once Room? waiting requests join Next step a new batch A short answer does not wait for the longest answer in its batch to finish. Two limits decide who joins: the sequence cap (max_num_seqs) and the token budget per step (max_num_batched_tokens). A third limit is not a setting: free cache blocks.

slides.title: The engine admits a request when its next chunk fits, not its whole answer
slides.text: Admission The engine admits a request when its next chunk fits, not its whole answer Admission checks the blocks for the prompt, or the next chunk of it, plus a small reserve. The answer's growth is not reserved: that is why the cache can run out mid-answer. A cap sized from Lab 1.2's arithmetic keeps answers from outgrowing the cache.

slides.title: A long prompt processed whole stops every answer in the batch
slides.text: Interference A long prompt processed whole stops every answer in the batch Prefill and decode share each step. A 5,000-token prefill makes one step last over a second. Every running answer waits for that step before its next token: a stall. Averaged over 150 tokens, a one-second stall barely moves TPOT. The visitor sees the whole second.

slides.title: Decode first, then fill the step's token budget with pieces of prompts
slides.text: Chunked prefill Decode first, then fill the step's token budget with pieces of prompts Decodes one token per running answer Budget left? max_num_batched_tokens Prompt chunk the next piece that fits Every step stays short, so no answer stalls. The price: a long prompt needs several steps to its first token.

slides.title: A block is reused only if every token before it is identical
slides.text: Prefix caching A block is reused only if every token before it is identical Each full block of 16 tokens is hashed together with the hash of the block before it. A new request looks up its blocks in order and stops at the first miss. Reused blocks skip prefill: a shorter time to first token and less work per request. So: one changing token at the start of a prompt makes every block after it a miss.

slides.text: Lab 4.2 · task 5 Route by conversation, fall back to the least-loaded replica def by_session(engines, r, state, limit=24): i = zlib.crc32(r.session.encode()) % len(engines) if load(engines[i]) > limit: i = min(range(len(engines)), key=lambda j: load(engines[j])) return engines[i] A stable hash, so a turn finds its history; a limit, so no replica takes a burst alone.
